answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is genuine. It comes from Stevenson’s essay “An Apology for Idlers,” first published in the Cornhill Magazine in July 1877 and collected in Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers (1881). The full sentence runs on: “… By being happy, we sow anonymous benefits upon the world.”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: There is no duty we so much underrate as the duty of being happy. By being happy, we sow anonymous benefits upon the world, which remain unknown even to ourselves, or when they are disclosed, surprise nobody so much as the benefactor.
trail: The exact sentence appears in the Wikisource text of the essay, followed by “By being happy, we sow anonymous benefits upon the world.”
A WIST catalog record dates the essay to the Cornhill Magazine, Vol. 36, July 1877, later gathered into Virginibus Puerisque (1881).
Because both the 1877 magazine printing and the 1881 collection long predate 1931, the essay is firmly in the public domain in the United States.
source.excerptNote: The line most people quote is only the first sentence; Stevenson’s point is completed by the sentence that follows it.

author.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
author.heading: About Robert Louis Stevenson
author.bio: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish writer whose novels Treasure Island, Kidnapped, and Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde became classics. Before the fiction made him famous he was an accomplished essayist; his early collection Virginibus Puerisque (1881) gathered pieces like “An Apology for Idlers,” a witty defense of leisure and unhurried living. Dogged by chronic illness his whole life, he settled in Samoa and died there in 1894.

misattribution.heading: Misquotes & mix-ups
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Stevenson is correct — the wobble here is in the wording, not the author.

items.who: “… the duty of being happy” (full stop)
items.why: Reposts almost always drop Stevenson’s second sentence, “By being happy, we sow anonymous benefits upon the world,” which carries the actual argument — that your happiness quietly helps others. The two sentences sit together in the original essay.
A common variant swaps Stevenson’s “underrate” for “underrated,” which breaks the grammar; the source text reads “we so much underrate.”

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Stevenson, from “An Apology for Idlers” — just usually quoted as a fragment. See the full passage.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Stevenson’s essay flips the Victorian cult of busyness on its head: instead of treating diligence as the highest virtue, he argues that being happy is itself a duty — one we habitually undervalue. The line landed a second time in the 1990s when Sarah Ban Breathnach built a passage of her bestseller Simple Abundance around it, which is why it circulates so widely on wellness and gratitude sites today.
